pron_note: Also heard as eks-KUL-payt; both are accepted.
means:
To **clear someone of blame or guilt** — to show they weren't at fault.

This is a word of *evidence*, not of mercy. **Forgive** leaves the guilt in place and waives the punishment; **exculpate** removes the guilt itself, usually because a document, an alibi, or a witness proves the person didn't do it. It stops short of praise: to be exculpated is to be shown not-blameworthy, whereas to be **vindicated** is to be shown *right*. Register is formal and heavily legal — lawyers, inquiries, board reports. Its exact opposite, **inculpate**, is the word for evidence that points the finger back at you.
trap: ⚠️ **exculpate ≠ expurgate.** *Exculpate* frees a **person** from blame; *expurgate* strips the dirty bits out of a **text**. Same *ex-* opening, entirely different object.
trick_unpack: The prefix does all the work — the shared middle *culp* is the blame, and *ex-* / *in-* simply point it out of you or into you.
sentences: The inquiry **exculpated** the engineers entirely, laying the failure at the door of the contractor who had signed off on the welds.
Don't try to **exculpate** yourself — I saw you eat the last slice.
in_the_wild: **"Exculpatory evidence"** is the phrase every courtroom drama and true-crime podcast runs on: in the US, prosecutors are legally obliged to hand the defence anything exculpatory — evidence that clears the accused.
etymology:
Latin **ex-** (*out of*) + **culpa** (*fault, blame*).

*Culpa* is a high-yield root: **culpable** (deserving blame), **culprit**, **inculpate**, **exculpatory**, and the confession **mea culpa** — literally *"my fault."*
one_line: To clear someone of blame, usually by evidence.
